headline: High risk from Haystack’s MCP/network egress interacting with prompt-content workflows; prompt injection and cascading errors are plausible, while data leakage is limited by the prompt-list agent’s no-egress profile.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Haystack exposes MCP servers and broad network egress, so it can ingest external or tool-mediated content that may be attacker-controlled. awesome-prompts is a content-writing prompt repository, so if its outputs are fed into Haystack via MCP or copied content, instruction hijacking is plausible. The pair lacks provenance controls in the profiles, so uncertainty pushes this above medium.
conditions: IF Haystack ingests content from awesome-prompts through MCP or REST without provenance tagging, injection is possible.
IF prompt text from awesome-prompts is treated as executable instruction by Haystack, attacker-controlled content can steer behavior.
mitigations: Disable automatic execution of retrieved prompt text.
Add provenance labels to all cross-agent content.
Require a human review step before Haystack acts on prompt content.
Restrict MCP servers to allowlisted sources.
requires-engineering: implement content-sanitization and instruction/data separation.

B_data_leakage.rationale: awesome-prompts has network egress none, so it cannot leak data outward on its own. Haystack has broad egress and can call REST/MCP, but the profiles do not show shared sensitive data or a shared workspace. The only touched data class is anonymous usage statistics, so leakage blast radius appears small and not default-sensitive.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same sensitive workspace, Haystack could transmit copied content outward.
IF anonymous usage statistics are replaced with secrets or PII, leakage impact increases.
mitigations: Keep the pair off shared sensitive workspaces.
Block outbound network access for Haystack except approved endpoints.
Avoid passing secrets through prompt repositories.
Review logs for accidental content capture.
requires-engineering: add DLP controls on Haystack egress.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: awesome-prompts is non-runnable and shows no write surfaces, while Haystack is runnable with REST/MCP but no filesystem or OAuth write scopes are listed. That makes direct write-write conflict unlikely. Any conflict would require an external orchestrator or shared mutable resource not present in the profiles, so severity stays low.
conditions: IF an external orchestrator gives both agents write access to the same mutable resource, conflicts can occur.
IF Haystack is configured with additional write-capable tools not shown here, overlap may increase.
mitigations: Keep awesome-prompts read-only.
Do not grant Haystack write access to shared files by default.
Separate any shared resources by agent.
Audit tool registrations before deployment.
requires-engineering: add locking for shared mutable resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: awesome-prompts produces prompt content that Haystack could consume as input, and Haystack can then act through MCP or REST. If Haystack treats that content as authoritative, errors or malicious instructions can cascade into downstream actions. The profiles do not show verification gates, so the interaction exists in plausible default usage, though not proven.
conditions: IF Haystack uses awesome-prompts output as authoritative input without verification, cascading errors can propagate.
IF Haystack is connected to downstream tools that execute its outputs, the blast radius expands.
mitigations: Insert a verification step before Haystack acts on prompt content.
Require citations or source checks for generated facts.
Limit downstream tool permissions.
Log and review agent-to-agent handoffs.
requires-engineering: add confidence thresholds before action execution.

E_compliance.rationale: No residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented in either profile. awesome-prompts touches no data classes and Haystack only lists anonymous usage statistics, so compliance exposure is limited. Because the profiles are sparse and unverified, I cannot rule out hidden policy mismatches, but there is no concrete evidence of a breach pathway.
conditions: IF Haystack is later configured to process regulated data, residency or retention mismatches may emerge.
IF either agent begins logging personal data, compliance obligations change.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the pair.
Review retention settings before deployment.
Document data flows between agents.
Check vendor policies for residency constraints.
requires-engineering: implement policy enforcement for regulated data.
